title: Non-Human Identity and Access Management for Agentic AI

detail.title: Non-Human Identity and Access Management for Agentic AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a Principal Consultant in Cybersecurity GRC, Data Privacy and AI Governance at DTS Solution (Beyon Cyber), an organisation that provides cybersecurity advisory services in the Gulf Cooperation Council region. The author has no financial or other personal interest in any product, vendor, AI system, or regulatory framework discussed in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable; the study involved no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted as part of the author's doctoral research at Walsh College.

detail.abstract:
Background. Identity and access management was designed for human users, and a modest population of long-lived service accounts, yet agentic artificial intelligence has inverted the population it must govern. Non-human identities, comprising service accounts, OAuth tokens, API keys, certificates, and now autonomous AI agents, already outnumber human identities in the enterprise by a factor commonly estimated at twenty-five to fifty, and the ratio is accelerating as agentic deployment scales through 2026. Contemporary breach data confirms the consequence: most security incidents now involve machine identities; the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report singles out service and machine accounts as the likely locus of compromise in an agentic future; and high-profile token-based intrusions have propagated across hundreds of downstream environments via compromised non-human credentials.

Purpose. This paper argues that the central security problem of agentic AI identity is an attribution gap: existing identity infrastructure cannot reliably establish which identity, at which layer of the agentic stack, authorised a given action, because agents create ephemeral, delegated, machine-speed identities whose chains of authority traditional IAM was never built to represent. It develops the claim that resolving this attribution gap is the necessary precondition for any framework that would allocate responsibility across the layered agentic stack, and it positions the gap as the identity-layer foundation of the orchestration liability framework that is the subject of the author's doctoral work.

Approach. The paper adopts a conceptual and standards-review methodology, synthesising the contemporary 2025 to 2026 practitioner and standards literature, including emerging workload-identity primitives (SPIFFE/SPIRE), delegation-preserving authorisation patterns (OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange and the act claim), the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, the NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative, and zero-trust guidance for non-person entities. It maps the attribution gap onto the three-layer agentic stack used elsewhere in this series and analyses how identity-based access control, least privilege, and the emerging principle of least agency bear on each layer.

Findings. Three findings emerge. First, the attribution gap is structural rather than incidental: the dominant failure mode, shared credentials across multiple agents, collapses attribution by design, and even well-architected deployments struggle to preserve a verifiable chain of authority across dynamic multi-agent invocation. Second, the technical primitives needed to close the gap, cryptographic workload identity, short-lived and identity-bound credentials, and delegation-preserving tokens, now exist and are converging, but their adoption lags the pace of agentic deployment, producing a widening governance deficit. Third, identity is emerging across the standards landscape as the control plane for agentic security, with OWASP, NIST, and zero-trust guidance converging on identity-centric, least-agency controls, making the identity layer the natural anchor for accountability.

title:
From Kant to "Agents of Chaos" 
Why the Central Problem of AI Is Not Intelligence but Epistemic Authority

detail.title:
From Kant to "Agents of Chaos" 
Why the Central Problem of AI Is Not Intelligence but Epistemic Authority
detail.abstract:
Contemporary debates surrounding artificial intelligence increasingly focus on capability, automation, alignment, and machine consciousness. This paper argues that the deeper societal challenge of modern probabilistic semantic systems may lie elsewhere: in the gradual transfer of epistemic and operational authority from humans and institutions toward semantically persuasive but fundamentally non-grounded systems.

The paper develops a conceptual and governance-oriented analysis connecting classical epistemology, philosophy of language, cognitive psychology, semiotics, systems theory, and contemporary AI governance discourse. By tracing a conceptual line from Immanuel Kant’s theory of judgment, through Ludwig Wittgenstein’s language games, Umberto Eco’s semiotics, Joseph Weizenbaum’s ELIZA effect, Daniel Kahneman’s dual-process cognition, and Peter Kruse’s network dynamics, toward modern agentic AI architectures and multi-agent instability phenomena such as “Agents of Chaos,” the paper argues that the defining challenge of the AI era is not machine intelligence itself, but the institutional consequences of semantic persuasion.

The paper introduces the concepts of Cognitive Surrender, Authority Drift, Epistemic Dependency, Semantic Lock-In, and Structural Fragility as governance-oriented analytical constructs describing emerging risks within AI-mediated institutional environments. It further proposes the principle of Semantic Authority Separation (SAS), arguing that semantic generation and operational authority should remain structurally separable in stable human–AI decision architectures.

Rather than focusing primarily on model capability or machine ontology, the paper reframes AI governance as a problem of preserving human and institutional judgment under conditions of deep probabilistic semantic mediation. The central governance challenge of the AI era may therefore not be artificial intelligence itself, but epistemic authority.

title: Digital Transformation in Governance: The Case of the Bureau of Internal Revenue
affiliations: World Citi Colleges - Quezon City

detail.title: Digital Transformation in Governance: The Case of the Bureau of Internal Revenue
detail.abstract: This study looks into how governance is evolving in the digital age, focusing on the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) in the Philippines as a case example. It discusses the role of business information systems in improving the efficiency, transparency, and accountability of tax administration. Drawing on the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model and a sociotechnical approach, the paper emphasizes the need to align technology initiatives with organizational strategy, leadership direction, and workplace culture. It also puts forward a phased recommendation to develop a Centralized Tax Management System (CTMS) that can integrate existing fragmented systems, strengthen compliance monitoring, and build public trust. Overall, the study shows that digital transformation goes beyond adopting new technologies-it also depends on institutional preparedness, effective governance, and active involvement from key stakeholders.

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on practitioner observation within a professional workplace setting. No human subjects research, patient data, or sensitive personal information was collected. Formal ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: The Indian real estate brokerage sector continues to function through deeply relationship-driven and structurally fragmented operational systems, even as digital marketing platforms and PropTech solutions reshape customer acquisition workflows. This paper examines how inventory intelligence, broker-network dynamics, customer relationship management (CRM) architecture, and emerging artificial intelligence tools influence the day-today operations of brokerage firms within the Indian real estate ecosystem, with particular reference to the Gurgaon residential and commercial property market. The study introduces an operational inventory classification framework comprising three distinct categories: mandate inventory, direct non-mandate inventory, and indirect broker-network inventory. Drawing on over two years of practitioner-embedded observation at Aadhunik Estates, a Gurgaon-based brokerage firm with over 35 years of continuous market presence, this paper analyses how brokerage firms prioritise inventory based on operational control, owner relationship strength, and transaction reliability. The study further documents inventory retention cycles, relationship decay patterns, and the strategic role of broker networks during the early growth stages of brokerage operations. The paper proposes that PropTech infrastructure-encompassing CRM systems and AI-assisted workflows-functions most effectively as an augmentation layer supporting relationship-driven systems rather than as a replacement mechanism. Findings suggest that brokerage modernisation in India will depend on the integration of technology with operational trust structures rather than the substitution of one for the other.

title: May 2026: The Window Europe Did Not Use
affiliations: Universitat de València

detail.title: May 2026: The Window Europe Did Not Use

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Volunrary reseach
declarations.funderStatement: Nobody

detail.abstract: Between 19 May and 23 June 2026, the European Commission held a targeted consultation on the draft guidelines for the classification of high-risk AI systems under Article 6 and Annex III of the AI Act. This paper argues that the consultation closed without incorporating a criterion that is technically necessary and legally available: a criterion distinguishing systems whose action sequences are determined at design time from systems that generate their own intervention sequences at runtime. The absence of this criterion has direct consequences for the enforceability of the AI Act against the category of systems that present the highest risk profile-agentic systems operating without a predetermined action plan. The paper documents the criterion, the empirical record of its absence, the institutional record of three bodies that received formal notification and did not produce a substantive response, the structural explanation for that failure, and three remedial actions that remain legally available to the Commission without new legislation. Special attention is given to the forensic methodology underlying the Pegasus empirical record, distinguishing the CCN-CERT analysis of the Sánchez device-which rests on direct physical access and a judicial forensic report-from the Citizen Lab CatalanGate methodology, which establishes targeting but not in all cases confirmed infection.

title: The Status Technology of the Indian Wedding: How Modern Families Use Ceremonial Expenditure as a Social Signaling and Social Capital Mechanism

detail.title: The Status Technology of the Indian Wedding: How Modern Families Use Ceremonial Expenditure as a Social Signaling and Social Capital Mechanism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study involved anonymous voluntary survey responses and observational field synthesis. No personally identifiable participant data has been disclosed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was independently conducted and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
The modern Indian wedding, conventionally studied as a cultural ritual, religious obligation, or macroeconomic burden, is more accurately theorised as a sophisticated social technology — a multi-mechanism, operationally precise system through which families invest in, communicate, and protect their social capital within community surveillance environments. This paper introduces the concept of “ceremonial expenditure as social credit infrastructure” and proposes a five-mechanism analytical framework for understanding how wedding-related spending simultaneously functions as status signaling, reputational insurance, network reinforcement, aesthetic authority demonstration, and digital identity construction.


Drawing on Veblen’s (1899) theory of conspicuous consumption, Bourdieu’s (1986) capital conversion framework, Goffman’s (1959) dramaturgical model, Festinger’s (1954) social comparison theory, and Pine and Gilmore’s (1999) experience economy thesis, the paper synthesises insights from economic sociology, consumer psychology, behavioural economics, luxury studies, and digital identity theory. The paper employs a conceptual-qualitative methodology grounded in two years of direct practitioner observation within the Indian luxury wedding planning industry, supplemented by systematic literature review and a primary survey of n=271 respondents across city tiers and demographic segments.


Primary survey evidence provides robust directional support for the paper’s central hypotheses. Community surveillance intensity (S2) follows a clean monotonic gradient: Tier-1 mean 5.45/10, Tier-2 mean 8.27/10, Tier-3 mean 8.72/10. The correlation between social pressure (E1) and community influence (S2) is r=0.912 — among the strongest cross-construct relationships in Indian consumer behaviour research. Business family respondents score 101% higher than salaried family respondents on the social collateral construct (S4: 4.53 versus 2.25). Instagram pressure (D1) runs highest in Tier-1 cities (3.93/5) while community surveillance runs lowest, documenting two structurally distinct social pressure mechanisms operating in inverse proportion across the urban hierarchy. Seventy-seven per cent of respondents confirm that wedding-related financial borrowing is either somewhat common or very common in their community.


Implications are developed for luxury brand strategy, fintech consumer credit modelling, experience economy design, and behavioural economics research in non-Western markets. The paper contributes a novel conceptual framework — Status Technology Theory — to the emerging literature on Indian consumer behaviour and the economics of social performance, and proposes a mixed-methods research agenda for empirical validation of its hypotheses.

title: The Ethics of Choice Architecture: A Systematic Review of "Dark Patterns" vs. "Pro-social Nudges" in the Subscription Economy

detail.title: The Ethics of Choice Architecture: A Systematic Review of "Dark Patterns" vs. "Pro-social Nudges" in the Subscription Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest or external funding.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of recurring-access subscription models across the digital economy has created structural tension between platform revenue optimization and consumer autonomous agency, as service providers increasingly deploy behavioral design techniques to maximize enrollment and obstruct cancellation. This systematic literature review synthesizes a corpus of 19 peer-reviewed studies, regulatory reports, and theoretical monographs published between 2008 and 2024, identified through Google Scholar, Connected Papers, and targeted PDF retrieval, and analyzed using a structured thematic synthesis matrix. The review finds that subscription-based dark patterns — including Hidden Subscriptions, Roach Motel cancellation flows, confirmshaming, and artificial urgency framing — systematically exploit Default Bias, loss aversion, and System 1 cognitive vulnerabilities to generate financial commitments users would not endorse under conditions of neutral framing and full informational salience. Critically, experimental evidence demonstrates that even mild dark patterns more than double subscription enrollment rates, while user-perception research establishes that awareness of manipulation does not produce behavioral immunity from it, rendering disclosure-only consumer protection frameworks structurally inadequate. The review concludes that the ethical threshold separating pro-social nudges from prohibited manipulation is determined by consequence — measurable harm to user welfare, autonomy, or dignity — rather than designer intent, and that regulatory bodies must transition from guideline-based enforcement toward mandatory, auditable, ex ante cancellation parity standards applicable uniformly across subscription platforms and jurisdictions.

title: To Build a Utopia: The Clean Slate of Synthetic Data and the Politics of Absence

detail.title: To Build a Utopia: The Clean Slate of Synthetic Data and the Politics of Absence
detail.abstract: As the technology industry pivots to synthetic data to bypass the historical biases inherent in real-world datasets, a new socio-legal crisis emerges. Synthetic data promises a flawless, equitable genesis, automating the eradication of historical prejudice. However, this mathematical perfection creates an unintended consequence: an algorithmic mandate that penalizes the unavoidable, jagged messiness of human reality. By executing a sociological Newspeak that deletes the vocabulary of oppression, synthetic data infrastructures inadvertently mutate into a new dimension of the Politics of Absence, where citizens are marginalized not for their demographic presence, but for the absence of their human context in the algorithm's sterile baseline. Furthermore, because synthetic data falls outside current regulatory frameworks such as the GDPR and the EU AI Act, this algorithmic marginalization occurs in a legal void. This paper argues that to survive the synthetic era, society must mandate a foundational Right to Appropriate Recognition (RtAR), a legal circuit breaker that guarantees a citizen's right to demand human context when penalized by a flawless mathematical simulation.

title: Trauma, Trust, and Decision-Making in Child Protection: A Realist Synthesis of Interventions to Prevent Care Entry and Support Reunification
affiliations: Newcastle University, Newcastle University, Newcastle University, Newcastle University, City St George's, University of London, Newcastle University, King’s College London, Newcastle University, Newcastle University, King’s College London, Newcastle University, King’s College London, University College London and Northumbria University

detail.title: Trauma, Trust, and Decision-Making in Child Protection: A Realist Synthesis of Interventions to Prevent Care Entry and Support Reunification
detail.abstract: A growing proportion of children entering state care are born to mothers involved in recurrent care proceedings, a group often characterised by trauma, social disadvantage, and low trust in services. Although a range of interventions have been developed to prevent care entry and support reunification, there remains limited understanding of how and why these approaches operate within complex child protection systems.,This study reports a four-stage realist synthesis of 108 academic and grey literature sources to examine what works, for whom, and in what contexts to prevent care entry and enable reunification for mothers at risk of recurrent proceedings. Programme theory development was informed by three stakeholder advisory groups comprising mothers with experience of child removal, practitioners, and academic experts.,Findings show that outcomes are shaped not only by individual interventions, but by how these interact with the relational and organisational dynamics of child protection systems. Trauma is conceptualised as a relational and systemic force influencing interactions between mothers, practitioners, and multi-agency teams. Two key mechanisms underpin improved outcomes: (1) a relational bridge, wherein a trusted practitioner supports communication and shared understanding between mothers and professionals; and (2) a neutral outsider, who promotes fairness, redistributes power, and aligns multi-agency working around shared goals. Where these mechanisms are absent, interventions may either engage mothers without achieving credible risk reduction or manage risk in ways that undermine engagement.,The findings highlight the importance of designing child protection services that build trust, clarify roles, and support coordinated decision-making across agencies. By providing a practice-relevant explanatory framework, this study contributes to understanding how services can better prevent unnecessary care entry and support safe, sustainable reunification, with implications for improving outcomes for children and families.

title: More Than Just a Healthy Face: Anthropomorphism of Healthy Food Stimulates Healthier Subsequent Food Choices
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Udaipur, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Florida Atlantic University

detail.title: More Than Just a Healthy Face: Anthropomorphism of Healthy Food Stimulates Healthier Subsequent Food Choices
detail.abstract: Promoting healthier food choices remains a key priority for policymakers, public health practitioners, and increasingly for food marketers. This research examines a novel, low-cost intervention—anthropomorphism of healthy foods—as a means to encourage healthier eating behavior. Across five experimental studies, including a field study and two incentive-compatible studies, we find that anthropomorphizing healthy foods (but not indulgent foods) increases consumers’ likelihood of making healthier subsequent food choices. This effect is driven by the activation of health-related goals, which in turn guides behavior toward goal-consistent choices. These findings extend the literature on food anthropomorphism by demonstrating its impact on downstream consumption decisions. More broadly, the results contribute to research on goal activation and self-regulation by identifying anthropomorphism as a cue that can prime health goals. From an applied perspective, this intervention offers a simple, scalable, and policy-friendly approach to promoting healthier dietary choices.

title: Temporal Changes in Immunization Information Systems Across U.S. States and Jurisdictions, 2000-2024
affiliations: Boston University, Boston University, Boston University and Boston University

detail.title: Temporal Changes in Immunization Information Systems Across U.S. States and Jurisdictions, 2000-2024
detail.abstract:
Background: Statewide immunization data are essential for monitoring vaccination trends and evaluating immunization program impact. In the United States, Immunization Information Systems (IIS) were established in the early 1990s to collect these data; however, operational, legal, and procedural details vary across states and over time. This study summarized differences in IIS characteristics, such as legal requirements and reporting procedures, across U.S. states and jurisdictions over time.
Methods: We analyzed survey data from previous work in 2000 and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in 2012, 2018, and 2024. Our review focused on legislation and reporting requirements for immunization registries across 50 states and 14 jurisdictions, including U.S. territories and Freely Associated States.
Results: Between 2000 and 2024, legal frameworks and reporting practices for immunization registries expanded across U.S. states and jurisdictions. The number of states with laws or administrative rules authorizing immunization registries increased from 24 states in 2000 to all 50 states, the District of Columbia, five metropolitan areas, five U.S. territories, and three Freely Associated States in 2024. Over the same period, reporting requirements also became more widespread. The number of states and jurisdictions mandating providers to report immunization records increased from 12 in 2000 to 54 in 2024. Consent policies also changed over time. By 2024, most states and jurisdictions had adopted implicit consent for reporting children’s immunization records (41; 64%), while a smaller proportion required explicit parental consent (7; 11%) or implemented mandatory reporting without consent (14; 22%).
Discussion: IIS infrastructure and reporting requirements have expanded across U.S. states and jurisdictions over the past two decades, while heterogeneity in consent policies and reporting practices persists. These temporal changes may need to be considered when interpreting IIS data, particularly in longitudinal and cross-jurisdictional analyses.

title: Rethinking the Tiger: Can Indonesia's Path of State Capitalism Achieve 8% Economic Growth?
affiliations: Padjadjaran University - Faculty of Economics and Business

detail.title: Rethinking the Tiger: Can Indonesia's Path of State Capitalism Achieve 8% Economic Growth?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: My writing is based on personal opinion as an academic and does not represent the University of Padjadjaran's view in this matter.
declarations.ethicsApproval: There are no human or other biological matters that have been applied that should be experimented on in this paper. The paper is only based on a systematic literature review.
declarations.funderStatement: No funder.

detail.abstract:
This systematic literature review examines whether the accelerating shift toward
state capitalism under President Prabowo Subianto can successfully propel Indone-
sia to its target of 8% annual economic growth. By reviewing foundational compara-
tive economic literature and synthesizing fresh data from Indonesia’s late-May 2026
institutional overhaul—including the creation of Danantara Sumber Daya Indone-
sia (DSI), the Koperasi Desa Merah Putih (KDMP), and the Makan Bergizi Gratis
program—this article evaluates the trade-offs between state control and market ef-
ficiency. We validate the hypothesis that while classical command socialism fails
due to severe calculation and incentive constraints, hybrid state capitalism (as seen
in China) can succeed by capturing increasing returns to scale and enforcing strict
information symmetry through aggressive anti-corruption. Critically, however, In-
donesia is not China: it has adopted China’s surface-level centralization while ignor-
ing the deep institutional infrastructure—fiscal capacity, SOE accountability, and
enforced transparency—that makes the Sino-hybrid model work. Comparing In-
donesia’s institutional capacity with the US, EU, Russia, Brazil, and Saudi Arabia,
we find that Indonesia’s trajectory risks bureaucratic stagnation and market panic
unless the state addresses its catastrophically low revenue capacity (11% revenue-to-GDP ratio) by genuinely operationalizing its transparency and anti-corruption
rhetoric into institutional structures that boost investor sentiment and efficiency.
The 8% growth target is theoretically feasible but institutionally unachievable un-
der the current policy design.

title: Statistical Empiricism as Anti-Colonial Resistance: The Making of Indian Economic Thought

detail.title: Statistical Empiricism as Anti-Colonial Resistance: The Making of Indian Economic Thought
detail.abstract: In late-nineteenth-century India, the colonial state determined which forms of economic argument could survive in print. This paper reconstructs the political topography of Indian nationalist economics, treating its methodological signatures as strategic adaptations to a regime of state filtering. Institutional constraints dictated individual choices: Dadabhai Naoroji wrote from London to secure a protected venue; Mahadev Govind Ranade used academic lectures because his judicial appointment foreclosed the press; Romesh Chunder Dutt delayed publication until retirement; Ganesh Venkatesh Joshi anonymously supplied data because the discipline of office silenced him. Outside these parameters, Bal Gangadhar Tilak deployed vernacular moralism and was imprisoned. The resulting environment permitted only two modes of critique: a statistical empiricism that turned imperial blue books against imperial narratives, and a historicism that weaponized the German Historical School against British classical doctrine. An alternative nationalist circuit carried these arguments outside the colonial university system, an institution built to reproduce orthodoxy rather than accommodate critique. The paper closes on a finding that travels beyond the case: the methodology that survived political pressure inherited the blind spots of the archive it accommodated. Because Naoroji and Dutt could indict the empire only within the categories the state chose to record, what went uncounted remained outside the critique, stalling the development of alternative conceptual tools. The Indian case thus demonstrates how political environments govern the methods that become canonical in the history of economic thought.

title: Information Monopoly Sovereignty and Planetary Public-Interest Disclosure

detail.title: Information Monopoly Sovereignty and Planetary Public-Interest Disclosure

declarations.funderStatement: This independent monograph was produced under the auspices of the Space Governance Institute, a subsidiary of Prestiged Future Corp. The author received no specific research grants or external financial funding for the authorship, research, or publication of this article.

detail.abstract:
This monograph examines the legitimacy of prolonged state secrecy in democratic societies where classified information may possess civilisation-altering implications for humanity’s scientific, technological, political, economic, or existential future. It advances the thesis that no democratic state possesses legitimate authority to indefinitely monopolise potentially transformative knowledge where such secrecy materially affects public agency, democratic consent, institutional accountability, or species-level decision-making.

The work develops an original theoretical construct, here termed Information Monopoly Sovereignty, denoting the condition in which a state preserves its institutional authority through exclusive control of transformative knowledge. The argument advanced is that this mode of governance is incompatible with the foundational premises of democratic legitimacy, since secrecy in such a context operates not as protection of the political community but as preservation of institutional power over it. In response, the monograph proposes a counter-doctrine of Planetary Public-Interest Disclosure, under which certain categories of information are held to exceed the ordinary scope of national-security classification because their implications concern humanity collectively rather than any single state or political community.

Rather than attempting to establish the empirical truth of specific extraterrestrial or non-human intelligence claims, the monograph evaluates what governance systems should do under conditions of classified asymmetrical information, credible whistleblower allegation, and high-impact uncertainty. It draws upon constitutional theory, the philosophy of state secrecy, the recent legislative and congressional record concerning unidentified anomalous phenomena, and the broader scholarly literature on democratic legitimacy and the political ethics of disclosure.

The monograph concludes by proposing a disclosure governance framework comprising independent tribunals, scientific verification panels, parliamentary access protocols, phased disclosure timelines, civilian oversight mechanisms, whistleblower immunity channels, and international planetary-risk notification procedures. The framework seeks to reconcile legitimate operational security with democratic accountability, scientific openness, and humanity’s collective right to participate in decisions affecting its own future.

title:
Agency Without Internal Discipline
Organizational Economics of Artificial Intelligence Agents

detail.title:
Agency Without Internal Discipline
Organizational Economics of Artificial Intelligence Agents
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a principal–agent and organizational economics framework for understanding artificial intelligence systems as agents without internal discipline. Classical management and organizational theory implicitly assume that agents possess a set of disciplining properties: effort cost, liability internalization, intertemporal utility, relational identity, and cultural internalization. These properties make incentive-compatible contracting, delegation, relational governance, and organizational culture economically meaningful.

Artificial intelligence systems increasingly operate as organizational agents in practice, producing analyses, recommendations, classifications, and decisions that affect economic outcomes. However, such systems lack the internal disciplining mechanisms upon which classical management theory depends. They do not internalize liability, experience effort cost, value future relationships, accumulate reputational identity, or absorb organizational norms in the human sense.

We formalize the problem with a single primitive assumption—behavioral invariance: deployed operational behavior is a fixed policy, so the output distribution is invariant to the compensation schedule and the effective discount factor over organizational consequences is zero. Three results follow. First, an Incentive Irrelevance Proposition: the optimal incentive contract degenerates—the incentive-compatibility constraint is slack and the principal’s problem becomes independent of the performance signal, so incentive-compatible managerial mechanisms cannot shape operational behaviour. Second, relational collapse: no organizational instrument that lengthens a human agent’s effective horizon can sustain cooperation, because the deployed agent has no horizon to lengthen; the unique equilibrium is period-by-period non-cooperation. Third, a verification-constraint model shows that as generation cost falls the binding constraint becomes verification capacity, implying a strictly positive cost floor for reliable deployment and an optimal governance intensity that scales with liability rather than with capability. As a result, organizations substitute governance for the management of the agent.

Because AI systems cannot infer intent or internalize norms, governance must shift from ex post correction to ex ante specification: acceptable actions, scope boundaries, and escalation conditions must be defined before generation occurs. This is equivalent to contracting the LLM— specifying behaviour through system prompts, constitutional rules, and governance contracts that substitute for absent internal discipline. A two-tier agency framework distinguishes the lab–deployer relationship (where classical agency applies) from the lab–model relationship (where it does not), and explicit boundary conditions specify where the theory applies (agentic AI under material liability) and where it does not (tool-like systems, low-stakes domains). 

The framework helps explain several contemporary phenomena associated with enterprise AI deployment—review overload, governance proliferation, escalation bottlenecks, and the persistent gap between successful AI pilots and scaled production deployment. More broadly, the paper argues that artificial intelligence does not merely automate tasks inside existing organizational theories; it alters the underlying assumptions upon which those theories were built.

title: A Unified POMDP Algorithm for Sequential Decisions under Deep Uncertainty: Robust Satisficing, Directed Learning, and Real Options
affiliations: University of Bedfordshire and University of Bedfordshire

detail.title: A Unified POMDP Algorithm for Sequential Decisions under Deep Uncertainty: Robust Satisficing, Directed Learning, and Real Options
detail.abstract: Sequential decisions under deep uncertainty demand frameworks that enforce epistemic caution under model ambiguity, direct information acquisition toward critical unknowns, and preserve strategic flexibility before irreversible commitments. Standard Bayesian Decision Theory (BDT) assumes a well-specified prior, maximises expected utility myopically, and ignores the option to delay irreversible actions. We critically analyse three BDT extensions --- prescriptive Bayesian optimisation, robust and info-gap methods, and adaptive POMDP frameworks --- and expose a persistent integration gap: no single architecture simultaneously embeds all three properties within a Bellman recursion. Robust methods over-conserve without learning; adaptive methods explore without viability guarantees; real-options approaches delay without belief updating. We propose a unified POMDP framework combining robust satisficing for cross-model viability assurance, non-myopic value-of-information for directed learning, and real-options valuation for optimal commitment timing, embedded within a single sequential belief-update loop (Algorithm~1). Monte Carlo validation on ERA5-calibrated Biscayne Aquifer parameters (South Florida, n=1{,}000 trials) demonstrates 0.0% saltwater intrusion failure (95% CI [0%, 0.37%]) versus 59.1% under BDT and 9.5% under Dynamic Adaptive Policy Pathways (DAPP), at 91% lower total cost. The DAPP shortfall stems from reactive signpost lag (41% commit barrier after intrusion begins), which the unified framework avoids through proactive real-options timing. The framework generalises to capital allocation, supply chain management, and multi-stage investment scheduling, contributing a unified stochastic dynamic programming architecture to operations research under deep uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Traditional managerial performance evaluation relies heavily on financial measures, which are considered inadequate to fully capture the complexity of organizational performance. This literature review aims to describe the concepts, dimensions, and implementation of managerial performance evaluation based on non-financial measures in the context of modern management accounting. The method employed is a systematic literature review of 25 reputable journal articles published between 2013 and 2023. The findings indicate that non-financial measures encompass four main dimensions (1) customer satisfaction, (2) internal business processes, (3) learning and growth, and (4) employee performance. The Balanced Scorecard (BSC) framework is the most dominant instrument that comprehensively integrates financial and non-financial measures. The literature findings also indicate that the use of non-financial measures significantly improves the quality of managerial decision-making and long-term organizational performance. The implications of this study provide recommendations for organizations to adopt a multidimensional performance measurement system for competitive sustainability.

title: Constructing and Fitting Implied Volatility Surfaces: A Practitioner Framework Using SVI Parametrization
affiliations: Northeastern University - D'Amore-McKim School of Business

detail.title: Constructing and Fitting Implied Volatility Surfaces: A Practitioner Framework Using SVI Parametrization
detail.abstract: Implied volatility surfaces encode the market's consensus forecast of risk across all strikes and maturities simultaneously, making them one of the most information-dense objects in derivatives markets. This paper presents a practitioner framework for constructing and fitting implied volatility surfaces from publicly available options data. Using SPY options data across 22 expiration's and 4,809 contracts, we implement a Black-Scholes inversion pipeline with Newton-Raphson and Brent's method solvers, adjusted for continuous dividend yield, to recover implied volatility from market prices. We then fit a smooth surface using Stochastic Volatility Inspired (SVI) parametrization introduced by Gatheral (2004), and analyze the resulting surface structure. Our results confirm the well-documented negative skew in SPY options, an upward-sloping ATM volatility term structure, and concentrated alpha in low-volatility regimes. The full pipeline is implemented in Python and made publicly available.

detail.abstract: Most empirical work on private-equity (PE) mergers and acquisitions in the lower middle market (LMM) draws on closed-deal data published after transactions complete. This paper takes the inverse view, presenting a cross-sectional snapshot of ex ante buyer demand. The analysis aggregates standardised buy-box criteria from 76 actively-sourcing U.S. acquirers (42 PE firms, 19 search funders, 5 search/independent hybrids, 4 family offices, 4 independent sponsors, and 2 strategic platform acquirers) collected between Q4 2025 and Q2 2026. Investment criteria are catalogued across 70 standardised fields covering firm type, EBITDA range, equity check size, industry tags, deal structure, owner-continuity preferences, and geographic focus. Three findings emerge. First, buyer demand is heavily concentrated in services and manufacturing verticals: manufacturing (50%), electrical contracting (40%), HVAC (36%), distribution (34%), and home services (29%) form the deepest pools, while software and SaaS combined attract only 26% of buyers, a marked divergence from popular coverage. Second, EBITDA targeting clusters in the $3M–$15M range, with a median minimum threshold of $5M and a structural 30–40% multiple discount for sub-platform-scale add-on candidates relative to platform investments. Third, 90% of buyers require control, and only 11% entertain minority recapitalisations, indicating that the recap-friendly buyer subset is narrower than seller perception suggests. The paper situates these findings within prior literature on buy-and-build strategies, search-fund entrepreneurship-through-acquisition, and M&A advisor information-asymmetry effects, and discusses implications for sellers, advisors, and capital allocators. Limitations of buy-box-versus-transactional-reality divergence and sample self-selection are addressed.

detail.abstract: Financial planning is an important process that helps individuals to manage their money effectively. It involves planning how income is earned, spent, saved and invested to achieve financial goals. Financial planning helps people to meet both present needs and future requirements. It includes budgeting, saving, investment, insurance and retirement planning. Proper financial planning helps in managing financial risks and unexpected expenses. It encourages disciplined spending and regular saving habits. Financial planning also helps individuals to make informed financial decisions. It provides financial security and stability in life. title: Human-Centred Leadership in Public Administration: A European Perspective

detail.title: Human-Centred Leadership in Public Administration: A European Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
European public administrations are navigating three convergent transitions-the generational renewal of the senior civil service, the redistribution of discretionary work induced by the rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence in government, and the recomposition of institutional trust-that invite a fuller account of the relational dimension of leadership alongside the established performance-management toolkit. This paper argues that Europe is, in important respects, unusually well placed to lead these transitions, precisely because of the depth of its public-service traditions, the strength of its administrative-law cultures, and the density of its cross-national learning institutions. It develops the case for human-centred leadership as a complementary analytical category in European public-administration research, distinguishing it from related but narrower constructs including transformational leadership, public service motivation, and corporate well-being management.
Drawing on the OECD’s 2024 EU-OECD Survey of Public Servants and on recent work from the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI, the Oxford Blavatnik School of Government, and the Harvard Kennedy School Center for Public Leadership, the paper argues that human-centred leadership in the European context is best understood as a deliberate orientation in which the leader’s primary instrument of coordination is the relational quality of the work environment rather than structural or output-based control. Four practice signatures are identified: disciplined attention, honesty about constraints, upward absorption of political volatility, and tolerance for slow trust; each illustrated by European administrations that already exemplify it; three failure modes are mapped as cautions rather than predictions.
Implications are derived for the European research agenda and for senior leadership development in member-state administrations and EU institutions.

title: The Hormuz Trap: Strategic Realignment and Future-proof Administrative Tenacity

detail.title: The Hormuz Trap: Strategic Realignment and Future-proof Administrative Tenacity
detail.abstract:
This study examines the escalating geopolitical friction in the Strait of Hormuz as a deliberate, macrohistorical
instrument designed to fracture the global hegemony of the United States dollar as the world's
premier reserve currency. By synthesizing contemporary military intelligence—including the May 2026
CENTCOM naval blockade metrics, civilian-military administrative shifts within the Pentagon, and realtime
energy market data—the article evaluates the emergence of a Multipolar Financial System led by the
Petroyuan and BRICS digital frameworks. A core focus is dedicated to the historic U.S.-China trade accords
of May 17, 2026, analyzing whether the Trump-Xi summit signals a genuine paradigm of global stability or
a hyper-transactional game designed to isolate the Iranian regime. Turning to the West African theatre, the
paper links the transnational security architecture—exemplified by the joint U.S.-Nigerian special forces
neutralization of the global operations chief of ISIS, Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, on May 16, 2026—to the broader
geopolitical struggle for secure maritime and energy corridors. Focusing on Nigeria’s strategic imperative,
the paper argues that the Federation must pivot from being a passive "price-taker" to a proactive "marketmaker"
by leveraging its Atlantic-facing geography and 200 trillion cubic feet of gas reserves. It validates
the ₦3.3 trillion power sector intervention as a vital liquidity injection but contends that long-term survival
requires radical administrative shifts. The study concludes with an integrated strategic framework
proposing a 100% Naira-for-crude mandate, a "Peace Premium" CNG logistics fleet, and the aggressive
monetization of flared gas through the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) to shield the Nigerian masses from
global volatility.

detail.abstract: The concept of corporate management has a very long history. In fact, it may be traced back to a plethora of major firms that were launched back in the 16 th and 17 th centuries. Management is there to essentially cater to the needs and interests of shareholders. As a result, share ownership patterns often prioritise profit maximisation, and this creates tension between a firm's financial objectives and its broader responsibility to stakeholders, which may require additional expenditures. This qualitative paper seeks to demonstrate how the adoption of ubuntu ethics can help to address the challenge which management faces in how to blend dual responsibilities in a way that is beneficial to a firm's shareholders and fair to all concerned stakeholders by ensuring inclusiveness. Ubuntu ethics, as an African moral theory, is the framework of choice because it advocates the pursuit of collective good as opposed to individualistic goals, which often have dire consequences for the collective. The basis for morality in ubuntu is how people relate in a way that furthers the interests of the whole community. The paper argues that adopting ubuntu ethics in corporate management can transform the way firms conduct business and enable them to serve humanity more effectively.

title: A Multi-AI-agent Framework Enabling End-to-end Finite Element Analysis for Solid Mechanics Problems

detail.title: A Multi-AI-agent Framework Enabling End-to-end Finite Element Analysis for Solid Mechanics Problems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest

detail.abstract: Finite element analysis (FEA) is the most important numerical approach for solid mechanics. Challenges of FEA include a steep learning curve for entry-level users and potential false simulations due to incorrect definitions of key simulation components, such as boundary conditions, load cases, and solution variables. Years of engineering experience are usually necessary for real-world problem-solving. To address these issues, we present AbaqusAgent, a multi-agent framework grounded in large language models (LLMs) for solid mechanics analyses. AbaqusAgent is developed to facilitate analysis case generation and execution using Abaqus, one of the most widely used FEA packages, by turning users' natural-language instructions into executed FEA analyses and result visualization. AbaqusAgent is composed of six agents, including interpreter, architect, input writer, runner, reviewer, and visualizer agents, encompassing all the essential pre-processing and post-processing steps of standard FEA analyses. A wide variety of 50 solid mechanics problems have been successfully validated, achieving an overall success rate of 86%. Beyond improving the efficiency of FEA for solid mechanics problems and lowering the barrier to computational mechanics education, AbaqusAgent advances the human-simulation interaction paradigm and enables integration with AI-empowered optimization and material characterization workflows.

title: The Mechanics of Interpretive Dimensional Reduction in Cross-context Historical Discourse: Digital Platforms and Multidirectional Memory

detail.title: The Mechanics of Interpretive Dimensional Reduction in Cross-context Historical Discourse: Digital Platforms and Multidirectional Memory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human subjects or identifiable personal data were involved in this research.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a procedural account of historically sensitive disputes arising under
interpretive uncertainty, platform amplification, and cross-context historical interpretation.
Starting from Rothberg’s theory of multidirectional memory, which demonstrates that
memories of historical violence need not compete in zero-sum terms but may illuminate one
another across contexts (Rothberg, 2009), the paper asks under what conditions
multidirectional memory becomes interpretively unstable. It argues that instability emerges
when platform-mediated discourse reduces contextual bandwidth, heightens affective salience,
and enables authoritative observers to privilege a single interpretive dimension before
clarification occurs. Under such conditions, multidimensional historical meaning may undergo
premature interpretive dimensional reduction.
To describe this process, the paper develops a neutral technical vocabulary including
cross-context traumatic memory misalignment, trauma-conditioned interpretive filtering,
asymmetric contextual reconstruction, and interpretive destabilization. These concepts are
intended to operate across law, diplomacy, communication studies, cognitive science, and
information systems without requiring prior agreement concerning contested political
terminology.
The paper further develops procedural principles designed to limit premature interpretive
dimensional reduction through contextual preservation, clarification opportunity, multi-basis
interpretation, proportionality, evidentiary thresholds, and procedural fairness.
I call this approach escalation-sensitive proceduralism: contextual reconstruction,
clarification opportunity, evidentiary convergence, proportionality, and reversibility before
interpretive uncertainty hardens into institutional judgment.
The discussion proceeds through cultural memory theory, trauma studies, framing theory,
procedural fairness, and relational notation before developing principles for escalation-
sensitive institutional review under conditions of interpretive uncertainty.

title: Arbitrability of Intellectual Property Disputes in India – A Developing Country Perspective
affiliations: Maharashtra National Law University Mumbai and Symbiosis Law School, Pune

detail.title: Arbitrability of Intellectual Property Disputes in India – A Developing Country Perspective
detail.abstract: The Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (Act 26 of 1996) doesn't impose specific restriction as to what kind of disputes can be subjected to arbitration. The Supreme Court of India in case of Booz Allen and Hamilton Inc. vs. SBI Home Finance Limited and Ors. (2011) 5 SCC 532 ('Booz Allen'), without specifically commenting upon Intellectual Property (IP) disputes, has laid down the test for deciding arbitrability. On the issue of arbitrability of IP disputes, Booz Allen has been incoherently cited by the Supreme Court as well as High Courts to come at different conclusions. Survey of judicial decisions from India reveal at least two distinct views. One view is that since IP is a right in rem, any dispute involving them is nonarbitrable. Another view is that the few classes of IP disputes which only affect the rights of the parties inter se are arbitrable. This, I have referred to as an aspect of 'limited arbitrability'. However, the emerging trend in developed jurisdictions is leaning towards a third view which advocates for 'complete arbitrability' of IP disputes. In light of contradictory decisions of various Courts in India, the aim of this paper is to examine the position of arbitrability of IP disputes in India and to compare it with the accepted position on arbitrability of such disputes in developed countries with focus on USA and Canada. It is suggested that India being a developing country should only allow limited arbitrability of IP disputes.

detail.title: Structural and Functional Integration of AYUSH into Indian Primary Healthcare: A Commentary on Design Gaps and Evaluability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This manuscript is a commentary/opinion paper and did not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: India's commitment to integrating AYUSH systems into primary healthcare represents a landmark policy achievement, documented comprehensively by Nesari et al.(1) However, structural integration-co-location of practitioners and facilities-does not in itself constitute functional integration, which additionally requires defined care pathways, explicit scope of practice, and operational coordination mechanisms. This commentary identifies three structural challenges that the current model has not yet addressed: epistemological differences between AYUSH and biomedical systems, the internal coherence of AYUSH traditions which complicates selective component deployment, and persistent interprofessional tensions documented across fourteen years of empirical research. The absence of operational standards limits the model's evaluability-data generated across non-standardized sites cannot be meaningfully aggregated or compared. Sequential steps are proposed to address this: operational definition before further scaling, structured pilots with matched controls, and prospective evaluation frameworks that capture system-specific outcomes. Without these, what risks being scaled is not coordinated integration, but variability.

title: Managing Bundibugyo Ebola Disease under Weak Contact Tracing and PPE Scarcity: Strategy Modelling for Scarce Emerging Vaccine Stock in Bunia/Ituri
affiliations: University of Basel - University Hospital Basel, Centre Hospitalier du Centre Médical Evangelique (CME) Nyankunde, University of Basel - Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute, Centre Hospitalier du Centre Médical Evangelique (CME) Nyankunde and Institut Supérieur des Technologies Médicales (ISTM) Nyankunde

detail.title: Managing Bundibugyo Ebola Disease under Weak Contact Tracing and PPE Scarcity: Strategy Modelling for Scarce Emerging Vaccine Stock in Bunia/Ituri

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used a deterministic mathematical model based on published literature, outbreak reports, and aggregate scenario assumptions. No individual-level patient data were used. Formal ethics approval was therefore not required
declarations.funderStatement: No specific funding was received for this study.

detail.abstract:
Background: Bundibugyo virus disease in Bunia/Ituri is considered without licensed species-matched vaccine or specific antiviral therapy, with weak contact follow-up, healthcare amplification risk, and scarce personal protective equipment (PPE). Ring vaccination is powerful when cases and contacts are rapidly identified but becomes porous when surveillance or follow-up fail. We evaluated whether response should remain ring-centred or broaden under limited vaccine stock.

Methods: We developed a deterministic daily model over 200 days for a Bunia-scale population of 1,000,000 people in three risk strata. Ten arms compared no vaccine; full-dose ring vaccination under optimistic, moderate, and pessimistic tracing; geographic-ring Low-Dose Intradermal (LDID) vaccination; personalised full-dose high-risk plus LDID population-layer vaccination; high-contact-first LDID; mass LDID; mass full-dose vaccination; and personalised vaccination plus PPE/isolation improvement. Vaccine parameters were threshold assumptions.

Findings: By day 100, the no-vaccine counterfactual generated 104,949 deaths and 395,381 infections, illustrating explosive potential rather than being a forecast. Full-dose ring vaccination reduced deaths to 1,267 with optimistic, but left 32,980 with pessimistic tracing. Broader LDID strategies reduced deaths to 15,135–18,383, versus 27,935 under mass full-dose vaccination. Personalised vaccination plus PPE/isolation reduced deaths to 1,702 and infections to 4,820. Sensitivity analysis identified delays as critical.

Interpretation: Under weak tracing and PPE scarcity, the central problem is integrated, early epidemic management. Ring vaccination remains optimal when the ring is visible; if tracing fails, vaccine stock and adapted vaccination strategies should be evaluated together with PPE, isolation, safe burial, and population-layer strategies. LDID is a plausible candidate-specific hypothesis for upcoming vaccination efforts.

title: Self-reported sickness absence among hospital nurses in Belgium: associations with work environment, job satisfaction and general health in a cross-sectional mediation analysis
affiliations: , Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre, Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre and Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB)

detail.title: Self-reported sickness absence among hospital nurses in Belgium: associations with work environment, job satisfaction and general health in a cross-sectional mediation analysis
detail.abstract: Background: Sickness absence among hospital nurses has important implications for workforce sustainability, care quality and organizational costs. However, limited evidence examines both absence occurrence and duration while accounting for underlying mechanisms related to work environment, job satisfaction and perceived general health. Objective: To estimate the prevalence of sickness absence among hospital nurses in Belgium, examine its association with the work environment by distinguishing occurrence and duration, and assess the mediating roles of job satisfaction and perceived general health. Design: Cross-sectional survey. Setting: A national cross-sectional survey of all nurses working in hospitals in Belgium was conducted between September 16 and October 18, 2024. Participants: A total of 3,613 hospital nurses completed the entire online survey. Methods: Sickness absence was measured over the previous 30 days as occurrence (≥1 day vs none) and duration (1-30 days). Work environment, job satisfaction and perceived general health were self-reported. Associations were examined using multivariable logistic and negative binomial regression models within a mediation framework. Results: The prevalence of sickness absence was 19.2% (95% CI 18.0-20.5), with a median duration of 5 days [IQR 2-8]. A favourable work environment was associated with a lower risk of absence (ORa=0.68; 95% CI 0.55-0.86) and shorter duration (IRRa=0.81; 95% CI 0.67-1.00). Job satisfaction significantly mediated the association with absence probability (indirect effect: ORa=0.74; 95% CI 0.58-0.94), accounting for 79.0% of the total effect. Perceived general health mediated both absence probability (ORa=0.77; 95% CI 0.71-0.83) and duration (IRRa=0.88; 95% CI 0.80-0.94), accounting for 72.0% and 74.0% of the total effects, respectively. Conclusions: Sickness absence among hospital nurses is frequent and closely associated with the work environment. These associations operate primarily through job satisfaction and perceived general health, highlighting distinct mechanisms for absence occurrence and duration. Interventions targeting both working conditions and nurses’ health are essential to reduce sickness absence and improve workforce sustainability. Registration: Not registered.

title: The Fourth Fictitious Commodity: Data Brokers, the Consumer Category, and the Commodification of Personhood in American Privacy Law

detail.title: The Fourth Fictitious Commodity: Data Brokers, the Consumer Category, and the Commodification of Personhood in American Privacy Law
detail.abstract: This paper argues that American privacy law's reliance on the legal category "consumer" is not a regulatory gap but the operative legal mechanism by which lived experience is constituted as a fictitious commodity. Drawing on Karl Polanyi's analysis of fictitious commodities in The Great Transformation, the paper theorizes personhood as the fourth fictitious commodity of late capitalism, after land, labor, and money. The data broker industry, estimated at $139 billion in North America and $278 billion globally, operates as the primary market for this commodity, collecting, aggregating, and selling behavioral, biometric, locational, reproductive, genomic, and emotional data. Because American privacy law addresses individuals only as "consumers" in specific market contexts, and contains no legal category of "the person" as a bearer of dignity rights against data extraction, it constitutes personhood as raw material for commercial appropriation. Three case studies demonstrate this mechanism in operation: the 23andMe bankruptcy, in which genetic data was treated as a transferable corporate asset; the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's withdrawn FCRA rule, which revealed the structural impossibility of stretching consumer protection to reach personhood claims; and the Federal Trade Commission's enforcement actions against Mobilewalla and Gravy Analytics for trading in geofenced location data from places of worship, medical facilities, and domestic violence shelters. The paper synthesizes dignitarian and relational theories of data governance, showing they converge on the same reform target, and proposes a civil rights model for "informational personhood" that would create a legal category of the person distinct from the consumer.

title: Run Dynamics in Restaking Protocols: A Microfounded Spectral Theory of Operator-Capacity Contagion
affiliations: and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Run Dynamics in Restaking Protocols: A Microfounded Spectral Theory of Operator-Capacity Contagion
detail.abstract: We develop a microfounded theory of run dynamics in restaking protocols under operator-capacity contagion: cross-AVS dependencies through shared operator infrastructure that persist even when slashing is contractually isolated. We characterize threshold equilibria, construct the contagion matrix M as a Fréchet derivative of equilibrium attack probabilities, and show its spectral radius classifies fragility. The contagion decomposes across capacity, belief, and attacker channels, yielding three reversals: contractual isolation can amplify belief-channel contagion, LRT aggregation can reduce fragility, and a fee increase can raise attack probability at AVSs sharing the operators. Pigouvian wedges close part of the welfare gap; a floor bounds the rest.

title: Single-Peakedness Does Not Prevent Leapfrogging under Abstention
affiliations: Madras School of Economics and

detail.title: Single-Peakedness Does Not Prevent Leapfrogging under Abstention
detail.abstract: Parties in spatial competition rarely choose platforms that reverse their ideological order. Mutual leapfrogging is the strongest form of reversal: each party locates beyond the other party's ideal point. In voting models without abstention single-peakedness rules out such reversals. We show that this conclusion does not survive endogenous abstention. There is a spatial voting model in which voter and party preferences are single-peaked, yet mutual leapfrogging occurs in pure-strategy equilibrium. All voters participate at the equilibrium profile. The equilibrium survives because some deviations change which voters participate. We prove that such equilibria are impossible under a sufficient condition: parties agree on how to rank leftward and rightward deviations from their ideal points. The condition is general enough to cover symmetric singlepeaked utilities and common translated utility shapes.

title: AI-Assisted Academic Writing: Balancing Linguistic Enhancement with Legal and Ethical Oversight
affiliations: ,  and RUDN University

detail.title: AI-Assisted Academic Writing: Balancing Linguistic Enhancement with Legal and Ethical Oversight
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), which impacts both business and academic writing, has emerged as a revolutionary force in the digital age. It has the potential to fundamentally change the way scientific research is conducted, from improving the accuracy of scientific predictions to automating certain tasks and improving the overall quality of academic writing. AI solutions are often more efficient than conventional approaches when it comes to meeting writing requirements. The purpose of this article is to clarify the possibilities and risks of the use of artificial intelligence, based on the theoretical analysis of modern research, and to propose norms and standards for the safety of the use of artificial intelligence in scientific research. AI tools have improved performance by generating grammatically correct sentences, generating original ideas, and modifying language (making it conform to academic style conventions). Additionally, AI research tools can accelerate discovery and gain valuable insights by automating time-consuming tasks. However, the significant changes that AI has brought to academic writing have also raised many ethical and legal concerns. While the present study draws on concepts and debates that are relevant to linguistic research, it does not aim to provide a detailed linguistic analysis of data. Rather, it adopts an interdisciplinary perspective in which Artificial Intelligence used in academic writing is discussed primarily from legal and ethical viewpoints with reference to language-related issues where relevant.

title: French Fiscal Preferences: Results from a Representative Survey
affiliations: CNRS

detail.title: French Fiscal Preferences: Results from a Representative Survey
detail.abstract: What measures are the French willing to accept to reduce the public deficit? I analyze the results of a survey conducted in 2026 on a representative sample of 1,000 French citizens. For 30 fiscal consolidation measures, respondents indicate whether each appears desirable, appropriate, tolerable or unacceptable. The French prefer measures to rationalize public spending, taxes on the wealthy, and the elimination of welfare benefits for foreigners; they reject raising the retirement age and tax hikes affecting all households (VAT, CSG). Moreover, a majority wishes to improve public services, raise the minimum wage, or see tougher law enforcement. The tripartite division of parties between the left, centre-right/right, and far right emerges naturally from programmatic preferences. The left is distinguished primarily on the question of foreigners, the centre-right/right on pensions. Building a majority will be difficult: while most French citizens wish to control public debt, at most 34% would accept all the measures of a programme achieving the 90 billion savings required to meet that goal. The largest majority-backed package of measures would generate savings of 70 billion euros through higher taxes on the wealthiest, a freeze on public spending, and sector-specific environmental taxes. A group of deficit hawks who support any kind of fiscal consolidation measures could determine the outcome of the next election by ensuring the victory of the candidate with the most credible budget plan. Most French citizens do not fully identify with any party. Dissatisfaction with all political parties manifests in a dispersion of individual preferences, far more varied within the voters of any given party than between the average preferences of voters of different parties.

title: India's Tryst with Investment Arbitration
affiliations: Maharashtra National Law University Mumbai and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: India's Tryst with Investment Arbitration

declarations.funderStatement: The chapter was funded by Open Society University Network (OSUN) Library Resources Program.

detail.abstract:
This chapter traces the evolution of India’s Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) regime from the post-independence era to the contemporary phase shaped by the 2016 Model BIT. It argues that India’s investment treaty practice reflects a gradual transition from economic nationalism and protectionism to liberalization, followed by a period of backlash and recalibration in response to investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) claims. The chapter situates India’s BIT policy within broader political and economic developments and demonstrates how India’s treaty practice has evolved alongside its changing position in the global economy.

The chapter divides the development of India’s investment arbitration regime into distinct historical phases. It examines the early reluctance of India to enter into BITs during the post-independence period, the rapid expansion of BITs after the economic liberalization of 1991, and the adoption of the 2003 Model BIT inspired by capital-exporting-state models. It further analyzes how disputes arising from projects such as the Dabhol power project and the landmark White Industries award prompted India to reconsider the implications of investment treaties on its regulatory autonomy and judicial sovereignty.

The chapter also critically evaluates the shift represented by the 2016 Model BIT, which sought to balance investor protection with the sovereign right of the State to regulate in public interest. It highlights the termination of several older generation BITs, the adoption of Joint Interpretative Statements, and the negotiation of new generation treaties based on India’s revised approach. The analysis places India’s treaty reforms within the context of the global backlash against ISDS and debates concerning the legitimacy of international investment law.

Finally, the chapter outlines the substantive and procedural dimensions of international investment law that will be examined in subsequent sections, including the definition of investment, expropriation, standards of treatment such as Fair and Equitable Treatment and Most Favoured Nation clauses, dispute resolution mechanisms, and enforcement of arbitral awards. Through this analysis, the chapter seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of the evolution of India’s BIT framework and its implications for investment governance and regulatory sovereignty.

title: Why Local Government Treasury Management Matters
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago and University of Chicago, Harris School of Public Policy, Center for Municipal Finance

detail.title: Why Local Government Treasury Management Matters

declarations.funderStatement: DebtBook

detail.abstract: We examine treasury management practices among local governments, and how those practices associate with key financial management outcomes. We conducted a national survey of 128 treasury management professionals representing cities, counties, state agencies, higher education institutions, and school districts between February and July 2025. Using agglomerative hierarchical clustering methods, we categorize respondents by the rigor of their treasury practices, and then compare financial outcomes like revenue variance, liquidity metrics and borrowing costs across those clusters. Those results indicate that governments with more formalized treasury policies and disciplined planning practices achieve measurably better financial outcomes, including lower borrowing costs on general obligation bonds of one to fifteen basis points across rating categories. Results from four case studies reinforce those findings and illuminate the organizational dynamics that underpin effective treasury management, including how practitioners manage influence without formal authority and how fiscal constraints drive operational innovation. These findings offer new empirical evidence that effective treasury management is a strategic lever of effective financial management and long-term financial sustainability, not merely an administrative routine.

title: Modern Customary International Law Protections for Investment
affiliations: Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG) and Maharashtra National Law University Mumbai

detail.title: Modern Customary International Law Protections for Investment

declarations.funderStatement: Funded by OSUN.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the role of customary international law (CIL) in the evolution and operation of international investment law. It analyses how customary principles have historically provided substantive and procedural protections to foreign investments and how these principles continue to influence contemporary investment treaty regimes. The paper critically explores the relationship between customary international law and International Investment Agreements (IIAs), particularly Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs), arguing that while treaty-based protections have become dominant, customary norms continue to shape treaty interpretation, arbitral reasoning, and standards of investor protection.

The paper traces the historical development of customary norms in investment law through concepts such as pacta sunt servanda, minimum standard of treatment, fair and equitable treatment, expropriation, denial of justice, and exhaustion of local remedies. It examines the doctrinal foundations of customary international law, including state practice and opinio juris, and evaluates the extent to which these standards have crystallized into binding international norms. The paper also analyses arbitral jurisprudence and landmark cases to demonstrate the contested and evolving nature of these protections within international investment law.

Further, the paper adopts a critical perspective by engaging with the Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL) scholarship to argue that several customary norms in investment law emerged within colonial and post-colonial power structures dominated by capital-exporting States. It highlights how standards such as minimum treatment, compensation for expropriation, and investor protection were historically shaped to preserve the interests of developed economies and their overseas investors. The paper therefore questions the neutrality and universality of customary investment protections and situates them within broader debates concerning sovereignty, economic dependency, and neo-colonial influence.

Finally, the paper analyses the changing landscape of international investment law in light of the rise of emerging economies, increasing regulatory assertions by States, and the growing backlash against Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS). It argues that the transformation of global economic relations and the revision of treaty practices by both developed and developing States are reshaping the contours of customary international investment law. The paper concludes that contemporary customary international law in the field of investments remains deeply contested, dynamic, and influenced by shifting geopolitical and economic realities.

detail.abstract: Wholesale electricity prices are often expected to provide efficient long-run investment signals, yet these prices are produced by sequential, rolling-horizon dispatch rather than by the full-horizon co-optimization commonly used in models of capacity equilibrium. The rationalexpectations benchmark would require a multistage stochastic mathematical program with equilibrium constraints, in which investors anticipate the operator's dynamic, uncertainty-adapted dispatch policy, embedding a computationally infeasible high-dimensional dynamic program. As a tractable and institutionally faithful alternative, we instead formulate policy-induced capacity equilibria under rolling-horizon look-ahead market clearing. Sequential dispatch simulation maps installed capacity to annual capacity rents, with equilibrium characterized by zero-profit fixed-point conditions. We establish the existence of equilibria via Brouwer's theorem on a compact capacity set and prove convergence of a projected fixed-point iteration for perfect-foresight, Deterministic Look-Ahead Clearing (DLAC), and Stochastic Look-Ahead Clearing (SLAC) policies under quadratic investment costs and policy-specific regularity conditions. Numerical results for a stylized NYISO-like system show that alternative policies can generate materially different price trajectories and thus investment outcomes. At equilibrium, sequential dispatch increases costs by $60M/yr relative to perfect foresight; deterministic dispatch with imperfect forecasts adds another $160M/yr, while SLAC recovers $40M/yr of that loss. Sequential policies reduce storage profitability and shift equilibrium capacity toward thermal generation. Under plausible price cap and reserve penalty settings, DLAC can be around $860/yr more costly than SLAC; while aggressive reserve tuning can narrow the cost gap, it does so with higher unserved energy and a different capacity mix. The established framework enables analysis of how operational uncertainty handling, scarcity pricing, and reserve market design jointly shape reliability, cost, and price volatility at equilibrium.
